claims.claim_vi: The source lists five common permission models: ACL (a list of rules granting or denying users access to a resource), DAC (access policy determined by the object's owner group), MAC (owners and resources carry classification labels), ABAC (permissions from attributes of resource owner, action, resource and environment) and RBAC (permissions from roles).

In Mandatory Access Control the operating system constrains a subject from performing an operation on an object; both subjects and objects have security attributes; the user cannot bypass the enforced policy, unlike standard Linux discretionary access control, which lets users make policy decisions; multi-level security implements rules such as no write down and no read up.
claims.verified_by: Read from a local clone of the repository.

claims.claim_vi: Observed with two unprivileged Linux users: a file created with mode rw------- was refused to the other user (Permission denied); after its owner ran chmod to rw-r--r-- the other user could read it. Linux file mode bits are used here, without ACLs (setfacl is not installed).
claims.verified_by: No external page reports this output; observed by executing the code on the authoring machine. The notebook describes Linux DAC but not this output.

claims.claim_vi: RBAC regulates access based on the roles of individual users; in Kubernetes RBAC permissions are purely additive and there are no deny rules.
claims.verified_by: Read from the Kubernetes website source on raw GitHub.

claims.claim_vi: ABAC defines an access control paradigm in which access rights are granted to users through policies that combine attributes together.
claims.verified_by: Read from the Kubernetes website source on raw GitHub.

claims.claim_vi: With Casbin 1.43.0: an ACL that lists individual users (a policy line for Lan) lets Lan read payroll, refuses Minh, and a new accountant Mai needs one added line per document (two lines for two documents); under RBAC the same Mai needs one role-assignment line for both documents; under ABAC a matcher comparing user and document department allows Lan and Mai to read finance documents with no added policy line, refuses Minh (engineering) and refuses a write.
claims.section: basic_model.conf, rbac_model.conf, abac_model.conf (models the demo is patterned on)
claims.verified_by: No external page reports this output; observed by executing the code on the authoring machine. Models were written for the demo, patterned on the repository's examples.

claims.claim_vi: ACL entries can name groups instead of individual users, and then adding a new person to the group is a single change that grants every access the group has. Observed with Linux file groups: a file with mode rw-r----- and group daemon was readable by a member of daemon and refused to a user outside it until that user was added to the group once.
claims.verified_by: No external page reports this output; observed by executing the code on the authoring machine. The notebook describes Linux DAC but not group behaviour. A NIST page on group-based ACLs implementing role-based access, cited by a reviewer, was not reachable and was not checked.

claims.claim_vi: A hand-written level rule allows a read only when the subject level is at least the object level and a write only when it is at most the object level: level 2 reading level 2 is allowed, level 1 reading level 2 is refused, level 2 writing level 1 is refused, level 1 writing level 2 is allowed.
claims.verified_by: The rule is the one the notebook states; the four outputs come from the author's Python function.

claims.claim_vi: ABAC only gives correct decisions when user and document attributes are kept correct, and complex rules are harder to read and audit.
claims.verified_by: The source says ABAC rules can be complicated and hard to implement; the dependence on correct attributes is the author's inference.

design_notes_vi: Một yêu cầu chung (Lan đọc bảng lương) đi qua năm mô hình, mỗi mô hình một câu hỏi; thẻ cuối nói mỗi cách chuyển việc bảo trì sang chỗ khác. Không dùng ảnh nguồn.
source_deviations: Source says DAC is based on ACL; the Linux example here runs on owner/group/other mode bits without ACLs, so the lesson does not tie DAC to ACL.
Source calls ABAC 'not commonly used' and puts MAC labels on 'resource owners and resources'; the lesson does not repeat either (unchecked; SELinux labels subjects and objects).
Source gives no cons for RBAC; the lesson compares the maintenance each model moves around, measured in the demo, and notes that Kubernetes RBAC has no deny rules as a Kubernetes property.
